correctness.rationale: The all-zero and alternating targets force at least 2m+1 zeros and m+1 ones. At the resulting length bound, a one at zero-rank c supplies exactly the eligible marker indices in {c−1,c}. Covering 2m+1 positions with m+1 such intervals leaves at most one excess membership, so repeated ranks are impossible, including at clipped endpoints. The first and last ranks are in {0,1} and {2m,2m+1}; jumps are one or two. For m≥1 this permits exactly two all-two sequences and m sequences with one jump of size one, giving the displayed distinct words and automatic avoidance of 11. The two m=0 words are immediate. To show attainability and sufficiency, pair up target positions consecutively on either side of the odd-index singleton assigned to 10 or 01. Each pair lies in {00,01,10}, all contained in 010; either singleton fits in the remaining block. Independently, enumerating explicit subsequence sets for target lengths 1,3,5,7 checked the optimal-content hosts and all shorter hosts of feasible length (python /workspace/reproductions/golden.py). The proof has no cutoff.

evidence: The prior one-marker theorem gives an interval criterion for arbitrary zero and marker counts, and classifies optimizers with each prescribed number of markers. Other general subsequence-universality papers require all k-letter words over the alphabet; the regular restriction in Adamson et al. is on the candidate host. Lagoutte–Tavenas study complexity for finite input sets in a different restricted-input problem.

At k=2m+1 and r=m+1, extremal full coverage forces exactly the length that minimizes cover length for the one-marker family at fixed r.
